claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
As-fabricated W–Cu samples exhibit phase separation and interfacial voids.
Phase separation and interfacial voids impede thermal conduction in the W–Cu composite.
The proposed intervention is rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering of the W–Cu composite.
Rapid liquid phase–assisted ultrahigh-temperature sintering will produce a transient eutectic or near-eutectic liquid at W/Cu interfaces.
Rapid solidification of the transient liquid will create a fine, compositionally graded W/Cu interfacial layer.
The solidified interfacial layer may contain minor intermetallic or solution phases.
The transient liquid phase will improve wetting at W/Cu interfaces.
The transient liquid phase will promote interfacial diffusion and homogenization.
Improved wetting, diffusion, and homogenization will suppress interfacial voids and phase separation.
The graded interfacial layer will reduce interfacial thermal resistance and provide a better heat-conduction pathway.
Treated W–Cu composites will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than conventionally sintered untreated controls.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will persist under service-like heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The process must be controlled to avoid excessive interfacial intermetallic formation or undesirable grain coarsening.
The hypothesis requires the transient interfacial layer to remain stable during prolonged thermal and irradiation service.
In a high-entropy metal-diboride/boron-carbide ceramic composite, rapid heating to about 3000 K formed a small fraction of eutectic liquid at component interfaces.
In that ceramic composite, cooling generated a crystalline intergranular dodecaboride phase that improved adhesion between the components.
The magnitude of any W–Cu thermal-conductivity enhancement and the long-term irradiation stability of the proposed layer remain unknown.
